text: The single theoretical result that justifies everything this course has been building toward: that scaling up a code is actually worth doing, provided one condition holds.

The threshold theorem says: for a given code family, there exists a physical error rate, p-threshold, such that if the actual physical error rate is below it, increasing the code's distance suppresses the logical error rate exponentially in that distance. If the physical rate is at or above threshold, increasing distance doesn't help, and can actively make the logical error rate worse. This is a well-established, proven result — the mathematical reason this field believes scalable, reliable quantum computation is possible in principle, not just a hopeful slogan.

The shape of below-threshold suppression follows roughly the ratio of p to p-threshold, raised to the power of d plus 1 over 2. Using illustrative values, a threshold of 0.01 and a physical rate of 0.001, one-tenth of threshold: distance 3 gives about 1 times ten to the minus 2, distance 5 about ten to the minus 3, distance 7 about ten to the minus 4, distance 9 about ten to the minus 5, distance 11 about ten to the minus 6, distance 15 about ten to the minus 8. Each step up in distance buys roughly another order of magnitude of suppression. Combined with the previous lesson's qubit-cost table, going from distance 7 to distance 15 costs roughly 4.6 times more qubits but buys roughly 10,000 times better suppression — a genuinely favorable trade.

If the physical rate sits at or above threshold, the same formula inverts: the ratio is now at least 1, so raising it to a higher power doesn't shrink the result, it keeps it flat or grows it. Scaling up above threshold doesn't just fail to help — it can make the logical error rate worse, by adding more physical qubits and more opportunities for something to go wrong, without the suppression mechanism available to compensate. Be precise about what's settled: the existence of a threshold is proven theory; the actual numerical value, and whether a given real device sits below it, is an empirical, hardware-specific, still-evolving question.
Next lesson puts this math to work on an actual question: how many physical qubits it would really take to run a well-known quantum algorithm, Shor's algorithm, at a scale that matters.
